summary: Describes alternate and additional mechanisms for MPLS-TP linear protection beyond those in RFC 6378, so that operators get behavior closer to what they know from SDH, OTN, and Ethernet transport networks. It introduces capabilities and modes, namely PSC mode and APS mode, and updates RFC 6378.

eli5.summary: If a road breaks, traffic switches to a backup road. This adds more ways to do the switch so it feels familiar to people from older telephone-style networks.

what is the mpls-tp ms-w command
subtitle: Extra MPLS-TP linear protection behaviors so operators of SDH, OTN and Ethernet transport networks get the switching they expect.

tldr.problem: The MPLS-TP linear protection of RFC 6378 behaves differently from linear protection in SDH, OTN and Ethernet transport networks, and in some cases can leave traffic out of service.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds five optional capabilities (priority changes, non-revertive changes, an MS-W command, protection against Signal Degrade, and an EXER command), advertised in a Capabilities TLV. All five together form APS mode, and none of them is PSC mode.
tldr.outcome: Operators can choose behavior that mirrors other transport networks. The RFC updates RFC 6378 and is itself updated by RFC 8234.

facts.label: Missing-message limit
facts.value: 3.5 times the long PSC message interval

today: RFC 7271 is a Proposed Standard. It updates RFC 6378 by adding the capability advertisement method, and it is itself updated by RFC 8234.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 6378 defines linear protection for the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP): two end points protect traffic by switching from a working path to a protection path, and they coordinate with the Protection State Coordination (PSC) protocol. RFC 7271 gives alternate ways to do some of those functions, and defines additional ones, so that operators get control and experience closer to linear protection in Synchronous Digital Hierarchy (SDH), Optical Transport Network (OTN) and Ethernet transport networks, defined in ITU-T G.841, G.873.1 and G.8031.

The five capabilities are priority modification, non-revertive behavior modification, support of the Manual Switch to Working path (MS-W) command, support of protection against Signal Degrade (SD), and support of the Exercise (EXER) command. A capability is an individual behavior and a mode is a particular combination of capabilities. Two modes are defined: PSC mode and Automatic Protection Switching (APS) mode. The reader is assumed to know RFC 6378.
sections.eli5: Two ends of a network line watch each other so they can move traffic to a spare line when one breaks. This document adds extra moves so it works the way people used to older systems expect.

sections.title: Why the Priorities Change
sections.content:
In RFC 6378 a Forced Switch (FS) outranks Signal Fail on the protection path (SF-P). That can take traffic out of service. When the protection path fails, PSC communication may stop, and an input with a higher priority than SF-P can leave the two ends in an unpredictable state. Appendix A shows a scenario: FS is issued at one end, SF-P then hits the other end, and after FS is cleared that end never sees the clearing message, so the two ends disagree on selector and bridge positions even with no real fault.

In SDH, OTN and Ethernet transport networks SF-P already outranks FS, and an operator who pulls a protection-path cable by mistake expects traffic to stay protected. So the modified order of local requests is, from highest to lowest: Clear Signal Fail, Signal Fail on Protection path, Forced Switch, Signal Fail on Working path. Raising the priority of Clear SF (SFc) fixes a second problem, in Appendix B, where a node recovering from failures on both paths could end up stuck in the wrong state.

With FS and SF-P swapped, traffic always moves back to the working path when SF-P occurs. For operators who want traffic to stay on the protection path even if the PSC channel breaks, the capability adds a local Freeze command that is not signaled to the remote node. It rejects further local commands and ignores condition changes and received PSC information until cleared. If Freeze is issued at one end only, a protocol failure can occur.
sections.eli5: If the spare road is broken, you should not be told to drive onto it just because someone asked. So the rules now say a broken spare road beats a request to switch.

sections.title: Revert Behavior and the MS-W Command
sections.content:
Non-revertive operation, from RFC 4427, means traffic does not return to the working path when switch-over requests end. RFC 6378 supports this only after a defect clears. Here a node goes into the Do-not-Revert (DNR) state when an operator command such as FS or Manual Switch (MS) is cleared, too.

That creates a need to move traffic back from the protection path while in DNR. RFC 6378 would require a Lockout of protection command followed by Clear, which risks leaving the traffic unprotected while the lockout is in effect. The MS-W command does it directly and corresponds to the "Manual switch-over for recovery LSP/span" command of RFC 4427. The old MS is renamed MS-P (Manual Switch to Protection path), and the Protecting Administrative state is renamed Switching Administrative.

MS-P and MS-W have the same priority. If a second is received after the first, it is cancelled. If two nodes receive opposite commands at the same time, MS-W wins and MS-P is cancelled. Both use the same Request value and differ in the Fault Path (FPath) field, which is set to 1 when traffic is diverted from the working path and 0 when diverted from the protection path.
sections.eli5: If you have moved to the spare road and want to go back to the main road, there is now a simple button for it. Before, you had to close the spare road first, which was risky.

sections.title: Signal Degrade and the Exercise Command
sections.content:
RFC 6378 only handles Signal Fail. This RFC adds protection against Signal Degrade (SD). How SD is detected is out of scope. The priorities of SD-P and SD-W are equal, and the first one served wins: once a switch has completed because of SD on one path, SD on the other path does not override it, to avoid switching that cannot improve signal quality.

While an SD condition exists, a node duplicates user data traffic and feeds it to both paths, a non-permanent selector bridge treated as a 1:1 architecture. In revertive operation the Wait-to-Restore (WTR) timer is used after SD clears, and duplication continues until the node leaves the WTR state. In non-revertive operation duplication stops at once.

The EXER command tests the PSC machinery without switching traffic: it checks the Local Request Logic, the PSC Control Logic, message generation and reception, and the integrity of the protection path. It matters only for bidirectional switching. A node that receives an EXER message SHOULD answer with a Reverse Request (RR). If both ends issue EXER, a node that gets EXER before RR treats it as an RR.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a road is not closed, just bumpy. The ends can now send traffic down both roads until things are better. They can also run a practice drill to check the warning system works without moving anything.

sections.title: Capabilities and Modes
sections.content:
Each capability is signaled by a bit in the Flags field of a Capabilities TLV, which goes in the Optional TLVs field of the PSC message from RFC 6378. The TLV Type is 1. The Flags field is a multiple of 4 octets, and a node signaling the five capabilities MUST send 4 octets. Unused bits MUST be zero. A node MUST include its Capabilities TLV in every PSC message it sends.

This is not a negotiation, only a check that both ends use the same mode. When a node receives a TLV, it compares the Flags with its own last sent value. If they differ, it MUST alert the operator and MUST NOT perform any protection switching until the operator resolves the mismatch.

PSC mode means none of the new capabilities (Flags 0x0), which is the RFC 6378 behavior. To stay compatible with nodes that cannot send the TLV, a PSC-mode node can send a TLV of 0x0 or no TLV at all, and MUST be configurable between the two. APS mode means all five capabilities, signaled with 0xF8000000. Other combinations are not supported by this RFC. IANA registered Request values 2 (Reverse Request) and 3 (Exercise), the Capabilities TLV type, and a new MPLS PSC Capability Flag Registry.
sections.eli5: Both ends hold up a card saying which extra rules they use. If the cards do not match, they stop and call a person rather than guess.

sections.title: Priority Logic in APS Mode
sections.content:
The Local Request Logic picks the highest local input. The PSC Control Logic then compares it with the last remote message and picks the top-priority global request, which drives the state change. A remote request ranks just below the same local request, except that a remote NR ranks above a local NR so a received NR can be used in the table lookup.

Equal-priority requests, such as SD and MS, use first-come, first-served. If a local and a remote request ask for the same action (same Request and FPath), the local one is higher. If a local request asks for something different from an existing remote one, the local request is ignored, and a conflicting local MS is cancelled.

When both ends act at once, MS-W beats MS-P at both nodes, and the node with MS-P cancels it and generates Operator Clear internally. For SD, the SD on the standby path beats the SD on the active path, so no unnecessary switch happens and traffic stays on the active path.

Defect inputs (SF-P, SF-W, SD-P, SD-W) are held persistently while the defect lasts. Operator Clear, SFDc and WTR Timer Expiry are not persistent. LO, FS, MS and EXER are rejected if a higher-priority local input exists, and a higher-priority request cancels a lower-priority operator command, which must be reissued if wanted.
sections.eli5: When several things happen at once, the ends follow a ranked list of who goes first. If two have the same rank, whoever spoke first wins, with a few tie-break rules.

sections.title: State Transition Tables
sections.content:
The RFC separates working out the winning request from looking up the next state. If the winning request is the local one, the table for local inputs (Section 11.1) is used. Otherwise the table for remote messages (Section 11.2) is used. States include Normal, Unavailable, Protecting Failure, Switching Administrative, Wait-to-Restore, Do-not-Revert and Exercise. Most are split into local and remote variants, such as UA:P:L for Unavailable due to local SF-P. Each state sends a particular message, such as NR(0,0) in Normal and WTR(0,1) in WTR, written as Request(FPath,Path).

The WTR timer starts only on a node that recovered from a local failure or degradation. A node entering WTR because of a remote WTR message does not start it. The timer stops when any request moves the node out of WTR.

For 1+1 unidirectional protection, which acts on local inputs only, the local table is reused, the received Request value is ignored and treated as no request, and the Exercise command is not relevant. The RFC's Appendix D walks through examples, one of which is drawn below.
sections.eli5: The ends follow a big chart: given where I am now and what just happened, here is where I go next and what I tell my partner.

sections.title: Mismatches, Failures and Security
sections.content:
In APS mode a node checks incoming PSC messages for provisioning mismatches. If a message arrives on the working path because of a configuration mismatch, or if the Capabilities TLV mismatches, the node MUST alert the operator and MUST NOT perform protection switching until it is resolved. A bridge type mismatch (Protection Type field of 2 on one side and 1 or 3 on the other) is treated the same way. If only the switching type differs, the bidirectional node SHOULD fall back to unidirectional switching. A mismatch in the Revertive bit lets the two sides interwork, and the node SHOULD notify the operator.

Two protocol failures are named. If the sent and received Data Path values do not match for more than 50 ms, the node MAY continue switching and SHOULD notify the operator. If no PSC message arrives on the protection path for at least 3.5 times the long PSC message interval (at least 17.5 seconds with the default 5 second interval) and there is no defect on it, the node MUST alert the operator and MUST NOT switch.

On security, the RFC states that it introduces no new risks, and points to the MPLS security discussion in RFC 6378 and in RFC 5920.
sections.eli5: If the two ends disagree about the rules, they stop moving traffic and ask a person to fix it, because guessing could make things worse.

fields.desc: Length of the Flags field in octets; a multiple of 4.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: One bit per capability; unused bits are zero.

items.label: Priority modification
items.desc: Swap FS and SF-P, raise SFc, add Freeze.

items.label: Non-revertive modification
items.desc: Enter DNR when an operator command is cleared.

items.label: MS-W command
items.desc: Manual switch back to the working path.
